item.research_question: How do small additions of hafnium (0.5 at.%) and molybdenum (1.0 at.) to the base high-entropy alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 affect microstructural characteristics and high-temperature mechanical properties, and can directional solidification further optimize these properties?
item.material_system: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (base), Al 9 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 Mo 1 (Mo-added), Al 9.5 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 Hf 0.5 (Hf-added)
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting followed by directional solidification using the Bridgman process (withdrawal speed 3 mm/min); homogenization at 1220 °C/20 h (Mo) or 1140 °C/20 h (Hf); annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests performed with a deformation rate of 1.3 × 10 −3 1/s in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C
key_findings: Directional solidification increased ultimate tensile strength (UTS) by a factor of 1.5–1.8 compared to conventional casting at temperatures up to 700 °C, while reducing standard deviation of UTS from 50 MPa to 16 MPa.
The base alloy annealed at 900 °C/50 h achieved a UTS of 840 ± 1 MPa at 700 °C and 575 ± 7 MPa at 800 °C, exceeding the yield strength of Inconel 617 by a factor of 1.7 at 700 °C.
Addition of 1 at.% molybdenum resulted in round γ′-particles and lowered the ultimate tensile strength compared to the base alloy under identical heat treatment conditions.
Addition of 0.5 at.% hafnium sharpened the corners of γ′-particles and led to a spherical Heusler type phase, resulting in the best mechanical properties among the modified alloys.
Annealing at 950 °C for 100 h increased γ′-particle size to 400 ± 100 nm for the base alloy but decreased the γ′-volume fraction by approximately 7–8% for the Mo- and Hf-containing alloys.

A three-fold reduction in Heusler type phase volume fraction (from 9% to 3%) in the base alloy annealed at 900 °C/50 h was directly correlated with higher strength, better ductility, and higher reproducibility.
At 800 °C, the polycrystalline base alloy exceeded the UTS of Inconel 617 by a factor of 1.2.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the strengthening to the presence of L1 2-ordered cuboidal γ′-precipitates and the reduction of the brittle Heusler type phase; molybdenum causes round γ′-morphology which is detrimental, while hafnium sharpens γ′-corners and alters Heusler morphology to a spherical shape with lower volume fraction, which is beneficial. Directional solidification eliminates grain boundaries inclined at 45° to the loading direction, reducing shear stress along weak boundaries.
item.limitations: The study notes that the base alloy and Mo-alloy with 950 °C/100 h treatment showed round γ′-particles which contributed to bad fracture behavior, and that large scattering in strain to failure occurred for samples annealed at 950 °C/100 h.
item.future_work: The top priority is to reduce or avoid the Heusler type phase to achieve a two-phase microstructure, clarifying its role on mechanical behavior and establishing the chemical and thermodynamic stability required for a spherical shape and low content (<3%).
quotes: The top priority for future work is to reduce or maybe even avoid the Heusler type phase and to clarify the question about its role on mechanical behavior.
Directional solidification (DS) showed an improvement in two ways as compared to conventional casting (CC).
The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase.
